claims.text: High-entropy solid solutions consist of five or more metallic elements in equal or near-equal atomic ratios.
The stability of equimolar multimetal nanoparticles is governed by competition between configurational entropy and element-specific mixing enthalpies.
Configurational entropy increasingly stabilizes a disordered solid-solution phase as temperature increases.
At low temperature, favorable ordering enthalpy can overcome configurational entropy and drive chemical ordering.
Ni and Si have a relatively large negative mixing enthalpy and tend to bond with each other.
Negative mixing enthalpies between particular element pairs can drive local chemical ordering.
Near 1923 K, configurational entropy will overcome element-specific ordering forces in the nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles treated near 1923 K will largely preserve a single-phase, chemically disordered structure.
At 473–700 K, the reduced configurational-entropy contribution will permit enthalpy-driven ordering or segregation.
Nanoparticles treated at 473–700 K will develop secondary ordered domains or precipitates relative to their initial solid-solution state.
The predicted temperature-dependent structural changes will produce measurable differences in catalytic activity.
The predicted temperature-dependent structural changes may alter thermoelectric or other structural properties.
Prolonged exposure under the proposed conditions enables thermally activated diffusion and atomic rearrangement.
The stability behavior may differ when composition departs from equimolarity or different element pairs dominate.
The ordering transition temperature and ordering extent depend on precise composition and processing history.
Identical samples will be compared after treatment near 1923 K and at 473–700 K for comparable durations.
XRD, TEM/EDS, and atom-probe tomography will be used to assess phase structure and elemental segregation before and after treatment.
Absence of a significant structural or chemical-order difference between the high- and low-temperature groups would falsify the proposed mechanism.
